doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Polka band beginnings and broad musical tastes
summary: Early polka band in Cleveland, the Beatles alongside Goodman, Ornette Coleman, and no gap between styles.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I’m glad you brought that up. The niche. You’re at the age where when you were growing up you could have latched on to some of the more contemporary musicians, and maybe you did, but the music circle that you seem to exist in is more of the mainstream type. What influences did grab on to you?

Well I actually grew up listening to The Beatles at the same time as I was listening to Benny Goodman. And strangely enough my first musical experience was playing in a Polish polka band in Cleveland, Ohio. And that was good training for jazz because that particular kind of music, it’s two trumpets playing in tandem and the clarinet improvises around them and you have four or five sections to each song and drum breaks and things like that. So it’s not unlike New Orleans jazz, as strange as it sounds. So I learned how to improvise just by doing it. I never took a jazz lesson in my life. But one thing about my family, they were always into all kinds of music and we were encouraged to listen to anything around the house. And back then and to this day I like to listen to all kinds of things. I was a huge Beatles fan and I still am. In fact I collect all these unreleased recordings and everything. And Elvis Costello I like. You know I listen to all kinds of pop music. I even like the music of Ornette Coleman, I’ve recorded some of his things. The mainstream thing, I just happen to like to interpret other people’s songs. Because I don’t consider myself a real great composer. So for me the interest lies in finding things that I can try to put my own voice to. You see my name a lot on these kind of jazz parties and things because I play the clarinet and the saxophone, but I do try to branch out a little bit more than that. I did a record in Bulgaria with an orchestra and we did some kind of twentieth century contemporary classical things and an Ornette Coleman piece. And I’m

really trying to show people in a way that there’s not that big of a gap between the music of Benny Goodman and the music of Ornette Coleman. It’s only a difference of — you know this whole history of jazz takes place, all the major movements, you’re talking about at most a 40 or 50 year gap of time.
Yeah. It really strikes me how fast jazz has moved along in its history and sometimes I wonder if it almost isn’t too fast.
